newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek court to try Moslem journalist over article.
newsitem.headline: Greek court to try Moslem journalist over article.

text.p: A Moslem journalist in the town of Komotini near the Greek-Turkish border goes on trial on Thursday over his writings, in a case that has prompted strong reaction from human rights and media groups.

Abdulhalim Dede, publisher of the weekly Turkish-language Trakyanin Sesi (Thracian Voice), faces up to three years in jail if convicted on charges of "spreading false information that may cause public unrest or shake people's faith in the Greek state".

Several groups have rushed to his defence, saying Dede's trial is an attempt to muzzle one of the most prominent voices in Greece's 130,000-strong Moslem minority, which has long been a source of tension with neighbouring Turkey.

"(The charges) seem to us discriminatory because they are being used exceptionally against this journalist, who is a mouthpiece for the Greek Turkish-speaking Moslem minority," Reporters Sans Frontieres, a press freedom watchdog, said in a letter to Greek Press Minister Dimitris Reppas.

The Greek office of the Helsinki Watch human rights group has campaigned to have the charges against Dede dropped and the Foreign Press Association of Greece (FPA) is sending a defence witness to Komotini in a show of solidarity.

"Our executive council decided unanimously to support our colleague, who has been a stringer for Agence France Presse since 1987, by sending a witness for his defence," FPA executive council member Rhea Sourmeli told Reuters.

Charges against Dede stem from an article he wrote in his paper, alleging that a local group of Greeks from Turkey was carrying out a campaign against the Moslem minority in Western Thrace with the connivance of local authorities.
Dede said he was charged after the group wrote a letter to the local prosecutor.
"By prosecuting me they are trying to terrorise Moslems in Western Thrace," Dede said.
Thrace's Moslem minority is at the centre of several disputes between NATO allies Greece and Turkey. Ankara insists they are Turks and that their minority rights are violated by the Greek government.
Athens says there is no such thing as an ethnic Turkish minority but a Moslem community of various ethnic backgrounds, remnants of the Ottoman empire which ruled Western Thrace until 1913.
Dede also faces on Thursday charges of operating a local radio station without a licence. Most radios in Greece operate without or with expired licences at the state's tolerance.

"Most Greek radio stations do not have licences and are never bothered by the authorities," the Paris-based Reporters Sans Frontieres said in its letter. "We wish to protest against the legal proceedings against Dede."
